passage:
"Vijay, why is the sink full again? I asked you..."
Ritu stopped mid-sentence.
"What?" Vijay asked, wary.
"Give me a minute." She closed her eyes. Jaw: clenched. Shoulders: up by her ears. Stomach: hollow. Breath: short.
"I haven't eaten since eleven," she said slowly. "And I've been hunched over spreadsheets all day."
"So... you're not angry about the sink?"
"A bit. But mostly I'm starving and tired."
Vijay laughed with relief. "There's dal. I'll heat it."
She ate standing at the counter, rolling her shoulders. Ten minutes later she said, "Okay. About the sink. Can we take turns?"
"Sounds fair," Vijay said. "And good catch."

qa.q: Since when had Ritu not eaten?
qa.a: She hadn't eaten since eleven.

qa.q: What did Ritu discover she was really feeling during her pause?
qa.a: She realised she was mostly starving and tired, with a clenched jaw and tight shoulders, not mainly angry about the sink.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Pausing to check her jaw, shoulders, stomach and breath, because it showed hunger and fatigue before she snapped.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when Ritu stopped mid-sentence?
qa.a: Vijay was wary at first, then relieved when she said she was mostly hungry and tired.

grounding: It shows a person pausing to check jaw, shoulders, stomach and breathing, discovering hunger and fatigue before they turn into snapping.

passage:
I learned the body scan from Vijay, the oldest cashier at our bank branch. He does it every day at four. I used to think it was a bit silly.
Then last March I nearly shouted at a customer who asked the same question twice. I went to the staff room shaking. I thought I was just angry at him.
So I tried Vijay's minute. Jaw first: clenched hard. Shoulders: stiff. Stomach: knotted. Breathing: fast and shallow. I realised I was completely worn out. I'd skipped lunch and worked late all week.
Now I do it at four too. Some days it tells me to eat. Some days to walk to the water cooler. Once it told me to take a real day off, and I did.
I haven't snapped at anyone since.

Sarika

qa.q: At what time does Vijay do the body scan?
qa.a: He does it every day at four.

qa.q: What did Sarika realise during the first body scan?
qa.a: Sarika found a clenched jaw, stiff shoulders, a knotted stomach and fast breathing, and realised the real feeling was exhaustion, not just anger.

qa.q: Why is the four o'clock check-in a good habit for Sarika?
qa.a: It catches hunger, tiredness or stress early, so Sarika can eat, walk or rest before snapping or burning out.

qa.q: How might the customer have felt if Sarika had shouted?
qa.a: The customer might have felt hurt or confused, since asking the same question twice isn't a big thing.

grounding: It shows a person using a one-minute body check-in to notice stress, hunger and fatigue before they turn into snapping or burnout.

passage:
Ward note, evening shift
I've been watching Swati, our charge nurse, do something simple before every handover. She stands in the corridor, closes her eyes for about a minute and checks herself: jaw, shoulders, stomach, breath. Today I asked her about it. She said, 'If my jaw's clenched, I'm stressed. If my stomach's hollow, I'm hungry. If my breath's short, I need a minute before I talk to anyone.' Today she noticed she was hungry and tense, so she ate a banana and rolled her shoulders before handover. It went smoothly, and she stayed patient when a relative got angry. Last month, before she started this, she snapped at a junior. I'm going to suggest the whole team try it.
Farhan, ward manager

qa.q: How long does Swati's check take?
qa.a: About a minute.

qa.q: What did Swati feel before today's handover?
qa.a: She felt hungry and tense, which her body check revealed.

qa.q: What does the body scan help Swati avoid?
qa.a: Snapping at others, by catching stress or hunger early and dealing with it first.

qa.q: How might the relative have experienced Swati's patience?
qa.a: The relative probably felt heard and calmer because Swati did not react sharply.

grounding: Shows a person pausing for a quick body scan of jaw, shoulders, stomach and breath, which catches stress and hunger before they become snapping.

passage:
Wednesday
Tried the one-minute body scan at 4 pm today, like the counsellor suggested. Sat at my desk, eyes closed. Jaw: clenched tight. Shoulders: up by my ears. Stomach: empty, grumbling. Breath: short and high. I'd been about to write a snippy reply to Mahima, my flatmate, about the dishes. Instead I thought, this isn't about the dishes. I'm starving and wound up. I ate the leftover poha, walked round the block and rolled my shoulders. By the time I got home, I didn't even want to argue about the dishes. I just asked her nicely. She said sorry. That minute probably saved us a fight. Going to do it every day at four.
Lavanya

qa.q: What time did Lavanya try the body scan?
qa.a: At 4 pm.

qa.q: What did Lavanya notice feeling during the scan?
qa.a: Lavanya noticed being hungry and wound up, with a clenched jaw and tense shoulders.

qa.q: How did the body scan change what Lavanya did?
qa.a: It revealed hunger and stress, so Lavanya ate, walked and then asked Mahima nicely instead of snapping.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt getting a nice request instead of a snippy text?
qa.a: Mahima probably felt less defensive and more willing to say sorry.

grounding: Shows a person using a one-minute body scan to notice jaw, shoulders, stomach and breath, catching hunger and stress before they turn into snapping.

Trisha: jaw: clenched. shoulders: rock. stomach: skipped lunch. breathing: tiny
Thomas: so?
Trisha: so I'm hungry and exhausted, and he's annoying, but maybe not scream-worthy
Thomas: go get a snack and walk to the lift and back
Trisha: ok
Trisha: back. ate a sandwich. I'm still annoyed but I can say it calmly now
Thomas: what'll you say?

qa.a: Arjun may feel a little embarrassed and more likely to listen than if Trisha had screamed.

passage: The lunch rush at the roadside dhaba outside Moga had lasted three hours, and Baljeet felt a snap rising when Lakshmi asked, for the second time, where the extra ghee tin was. Instead of answering, Baljeet did what had become a habit since winter: stepped behind the tandoor, closed both eyes for a minute and checked. Jaw clenched. Shoulders up. Stomach hollow. Breath short and high. "You haven't eaten since six," Baljeet muttered, "and you're tired, not angry at her." A plate of dal and two rotis, eaten standing, and a slow breath out. Then back to the counter. "Ghee's under the bench, left side. Sorry, I was about to bite your head off." Lakshmi laughed. "I saw. Go on, eat another roti."

qa.q: Where is the extra ghee tin?
qa.a: Under the bench, on the left side.

qa.q: What was Baljeet really feeling when the snap rose, and how did the check show it?
qa.a: The clenched jaw, raised shoulders, hollow stomach and short breath showed Baljeet was hungry and tired, not truly angry at Lakshmi.

qa.q: Why is this one-minute check a useful habit?
qa.a: It catches hunger, stress and fatigue before they turn into snapping, so Baljeet can eat, breathe and answer kindly.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt if Baljeet had snapped instead?
qa.a: Lakshmi would likely have felt hurt or annoyed over a simple question, and the rush would have felt even harder.

grounding: Shows a person pausing for a minute to notice jaw, shoulders, stomach and breathing, and catching hunger and fatigue before they turn into snapping.
